options.text: A connectionless, best-effort transport with no delivery guarantee
A routing protocol for the internet core

questions.explanation: UDP sends independent datagrams with no handshake, ordering, or retransmission — it is connectionless and best-effort.

questions.prompt: Which guarantees does UDP NOT provide? Select all that apply.

options.text: Port numbers to reach the right application

questions.explanation: UDP omits retransmission, ordering, and any handshake. It does still have ports (source and destination) to reach the right application.

questions.prompt: UDP's protocol data unit — a self-contained message with no relationship to others — is called a ____.
questions.explanation: UDP sends datagrams, each independent of the others, unlike TCP's continuous byte stream.

questions.prompt: Why might a live video call prefer UDP over TCP?

options.text: A frame that arrives late is useless, so it's better to drop loss and keep going
UDP guarantees every frame arrives in order
TCP cannot carry audio or video

questions.explanation: Real-time media values timeliness over completeness; retransmitting a late frame would only stall the stream, so UDP's fire-and-forget model fits.

questions.prompt: Match each application to why it uses UDP.

pairs.right: One small question and answer, no handshake needed
Broadcast-based config before the host has an IP
Builds its own reliability and encryption over UDP

questions.explanation: DNS and DHCP are lightweight request/response, real-time media favors low latency, and QUIC reimplements reliability atop UDP.

questions.prompt: Order these transports from smallest to largest minimum header size.
questions.explanation: UDP's header is 8 bytes; TCP's minimum header is 20 bytes, which is part of why UDP is favored for high-rate, low-latency traffic.
